lines.text: אגר 11 אגן
* אָגַד obsol. root, Chald. to bind, to tie,
comp. אָכַד, עָקַד, and the remark under
r. גִּיד. In Arabic some of its derivatives
are used trop. of arched work, edifices
of arched and firmly compacted struc-
ture, in reference to the firm coherence
of all their parts; comp. אָחַז and אֲגֻדָּה
no. 4.—Hence
אֲגֻדָּה f. 1. a band, knot. אֲגֻדּוֹת מוֹטָה
bands of the yoke, Is. 58, 6.
2. a bundle, bunch, tied together, e. g.
of hyssop, Ex. 12, 22.
3. a band of men, troop, 2 Sam. 2, 25.
Comp. חֶבֶל.
4. an arch, vault, e. g. of the heavens,
Am. 9, 6. Comp. Germ. Gat, Gaden,
story of a building, from the verb gaden,
gatten, which implies a binding; see
Adelung Lex. h. vv.
אֱגוֹז m. a nut, Cant. 6, 11. Syr. and
Arab. جَوْز, ܓܰܘܙܳܐ, Pers. گوز. The
Heb. word seems derived from the Per-
sian, prefixing א prosthetic. Comp. in
lett. א.
אָגוּר Agur, pr. n. of a wise man, the
son of Jakeh, יָקֶה, to whom the 30th
chapter of Proverbs is ascribed, v. 1. If
the name be symbolical, like Koheleth,
it may denote an assembler, one of the
assembly, sc. of wise men, i. q. בַּעַל אֲסֻפָּה
אֲגוֹרָה f. a small coin, piece of money,
penny, so called from the idea of collect-
ing, from r. אָגַר; as Lat. stips in the
phrase stipem colligere. 1 Sam. 2, 36.
In the Maltese idiom, agar denotes the
same. [Or perh. pr. hire, wages, from r.
אָגַר no. 2, comp. Syr. ܐܰܓܽܘܪܬܳܐ Is. 23, 18;
then money, 1 Sam. 2, 36, where too Syr.
ܐܰܓܽܘܪܬܳܐ.—T.] Sept. Vulg. ὀβολός, num-
mus. Rabb. גֵּרָה q. v.
* אָגַל obsol. root, pr. to flow together,
to be collected, as water, kindr. with r.
גָּלַל, which is also used of the rolling
waves; comp. in אָגַר. Arab. أَجَّلَ Conj.
II. to make flow together, hence to collect
water; مَأْجَلٌ standing water, a pond,
reservoir; comp. also אָגַר.—Hence
אֶגֶל, Job 38, 28 אֶגְלֵי טַל the reservoirs
of the dew, i. e. in the heavens; comp. in
v. 22 the storehouses of the snow and
hail.—Vulg. Chald. Syr. give it by drops
of the dew, q. d. globules, comp. גְּלַל; but
the former is better.
אֶגְלַיִם (two ponds) Is. 15, 8 Eglaim,
pr. n. of a village in the territory of Moab,
the Ἀγαλλείμ of Eusebius, called by Jo-
sephus Ἄγαλλα, Ant. 14. 1. 4.
* אָגַם obsol. root; in Arabic:
1. Mid. A, to burn, to be hot, comp.
חָמַם, יָחַם. Hence אַגְמוֹן no. 1.
2. Mid. E, to be warm, spoiled, dead,
hence אָגֵם.
as water; hence אֲגַם and אַגְמוֹן no. 2.
3. Mid. E, to loathe, to abhor, and
Chald. אֲגַם to be pained, sad, to grieve;
אֲגַם m. (r. אָגַם no. 2) absol. Is. 35, 7;
constr. 41, 18. Ps. 107, 35; plur. אֲגַמִּים,
constr. אַגְמֵי.
1. stagnant water, a pool, marsh, Is.
the pools of stagnant water left by the
Nile after its inundation, Ex. 7, 19.
2. i. q. אַגְמוֹן, a reed, cane, Jer. 51, 32,
with which fortifications (stockades, pa-
lisades) were constructed. Hence R.
Jonah explains it strong-holds; comp.
أَجَمَةٌ the marshy lair of the lion. then
a refuge, strong-hold.
אָגֵם adj. once in plur. constr. אַגְמֵי נֶפֶשׁ
sad, sorrowful in mind, Is. 19, 10. R.
אָגַם no. 3.
אַגְמוֹן, אַגְמֹן, m. (r. אָגַם) 1. a caldron,
heated kettle, Job. 41, 12 [20]. Others
translate the words כְּדוּד נָפוּחַ וְאַגְמוֹן
as a boiling pot and a (burning) reed.
See the root no. 1.
2. a reed, bulrush, growing in marsh
es, from אֲגַם marsh, and the ending וֹן,
כִּפָּה.—Hence
3. a rope made of reeds; a rush-cord,
like Gr. σχοῖνος, Job 40, 26 [41, 2].
Comp. Plin. H. N. 19. 2.
* אָגַן obsol. root; Arab. أَجَنَ i. q.
وجن (see יָגַן) to tread with the feet,
to stamp, to beat; then to wash clothes, to
full, as a washer or fuller by treading
them in a trough.—Hence

line_status.note: The left header word's final letter has a rounded shoulder with no right-side tittle projecting past the leg, so it is resh (אגר), not dalet (אגד). Page number 11 and right header אגן agree in both readings.

The prefixed mark is a radiating star-shaped asterisk (several short strokes/dots around a centre), not a dagger with a vertical stem and crossbar; Robinson's edition uses * for obsolete roots. Headword אָגַד (qamets, pathach, no plene letters) and the English text agree in both readings.

Printed left-to-right order is אָכַד first, then עָקַד (Reading A reverses them). The second letter of the first word is kaf (rounded, no lower-right protrusion), not bet — so אָכַד as in B; vowels qamets + patach on both words match.
The Persian word carries only the three dots marking gāf above the kāf, no fatḥa; Reading A's گَوز adds a vowel that is not printed. Arabic and Syriac items match both readings.

The Syriac word is printed plene with vav: an x-shaped esoso (ܽ) is clearly visible over the gamal/vav in the middle of the word, and the vav loop is present between gamal's tail and resh; Reading A omits both. Ptoho over alaph and zqofo over taw are printed as in B. Single space after "2,".

The Syriac word is printed plene with waw: a loop glyph with the esasa (u) vowel sits between gamal and resh, giving ܐܰܓܽܘܪܬܳܐ (agurto), not the defective ܐܓܪܬܐ of Reading A. The remainder of the line is identical in both readings; the gap after "T.]" is just a wide space, written here as a single space.
The jim is printed with a shadda (plus fatha) above it, as expected for the Conj. II form; Reading A omits the shadda. Hebrew אָגַר and the rest of the line are identical in both.

The lām clearly carries a tanwīn (ٌ, the "9"-shaped mark above it), so Reading A's مَأْجَل is defective; but the print also has a space before the semicolon ("water ;"), which Reading B drops. Correct line combines A's spacing with B's Arabic.

Under the aleph of the headword the print shows three dots in a triangle (segol), matching the segol under the gimel, not the two horizontal dots of tsere; the rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.
The point under the gimel is a narrow vertical mark (two stacked dots = shewa), not the wide T-shaped qamets of Reading A; dagesh in gimel and patah under the first lamed as in both readings.
No maqqef is printed between אַגְמֵי and נֶפֶשׁ — the two words are separated by a plain space with no horizontal stroke at the top of the gap, so Reading B is correct.

The leftmost (first) Hebrew item in the printed line is the plene form with vav (אַגְמוֹן, five letters), and the second is defective אַגְמֹן (four letters, holem alone over mem); Reading A reverses this order. Root אָגַם and the rest agree with both readings.
After "reeds" the mark has a distinct dot above the comma-shaped tail, so it is a semicolon, not a comma; Reading B is correct.

The rightmost Hebrew letter in the parenthesis is a short glyph that stops well above the baseline (a yod), not a full-height resh; the qamets sits clearly below it with a gap. Everything else (Arabic وجن, patach on gimel, final nun, English) matches both readings.
